# Technical Brief: Compiler Internals Optimization

## 1. SSA Construction

**Dominance-frontier construction (Cytron-Ferrante-Rosen-Wegman-Zadeck, 1991).** The canonical algorithm builds a dominator tree, then for each definition site computes the iterated dominance frontier (IDF) — the minimal set of join points where competing definitions require a φ-node. A node *n* is in the dominance frontier of *d* if *d* dominates a predecessor of *n* but does not strictly dominate *n* itself. Iterating this set until fixpoint yields placement for all necessary φ-nodes, producing *minimal SSA* (every φ-node has a distinct set of reaching definitions, though some may be dead). Pruned SSA refines this by inserting φ-nodes only for variables actually live across the join point, using a prior liveness analysis — avoiding φ-nodes for variables that are never used after the merge. This is the construction strategy historically used in GCC's GIMPLE SSA form and in early LLVM passes (`mem2reg`-adjacent construction).

**Braun et al.'s simple and efficient SSA construction (2013).** Instead of computing dominance frontiers up front, this algorithm builds SSA incrementally during a single pass over the CFG, using local value numbering per block: each variable read looks up the current definition in the block; if none exists locally, it recurses into predecessors. Blocks not yet fully constructed (because not all predecessors are known, e.g., forward branches/loops) are marked *unsealed* and receive an *incomplete φ-node* as a placeholder, which is later completed once the block seals. A separate pass removes trivial/redundant φ-nodes (a φ-node whose operands are all the same value, or that self-references, can be replaced by that value). This avoids the separate dominance/liveness analyses, trading a slightly more complex incremental bookkeeping (tracking sealed/unsealed blocks and per-block variable maps) for simplicity of implementation; it's used in Cranelift's SSA builder and various educational/production JIT front-ends.

**SSA destruction.** Converting back to non-SSA form before register allocation (or in the back-end) must resolve the semantics of φ-nodes, which notionally perform simultaneous assignment on entry to a block from each predecessor. Naively lowering φ-nodes to copies at the end of each predecessor block is unsound in the presence of the *lost-copy problem* and the *swap problem*: if two variables are exchanged across a loop back-edge, sequential copy insertion can clobber a value before it is read. The standard fix (Sreedhar et al.; also described by Boissinot et al.) computes *parallel copies* at each predecessor and sequentializes them correctly, inserting temporaries to break cycles. SSA destruction also defines *φ-congruence classes* — the transitive closure of variables connected by φ-node operands that may be coalesced into a single storage location — and this coalescing interacts directly with register allocation's own coalescing phase (see below). Sea-of-nodes IRs (HotSpot C2, V8 Turbofan, Graal) sidestep explicit φ bookkeeping differently — φ-nodes are ordinary graph nodes merged at region nodes, and scheduling (not a separate SSA-destruction pass) linearizes the graph into blocks.

## 2. Alias Analysis

**Andersen's analysis.** An inclusion-based (subset-constraint) points-to analysis: each pointer variable is modeled as a set variable, and assignments generate subset constraints (e.g., `p = q` generates pts(q) ⊆ pts(p)). Constraints are solved to a fixpoint, typically via a worklist propagating points-to set elements along the constraint graph. It is flow-insensitive (ignores statement order) and context-insensitive by default, with worst-case cubic complexity O(n³) in the number of variables, though practical implementations with online cycle-elimination and sparse bitsets scale better. It is strictly more precise than Steensgaard's analysis because each variable gets its own points-to set rather than being unified with everything it's ever assigned to or from.

**Steensgaard's analysis.** A unification-based points-to analysis: whenever `p` and `q` are related by an assignment, their "representative" abstract locations are unified using a union-find structure, so all aliasing relationships collapse into equivalence classes. This yields near-linear time (close to O(n) with near-constant-time union-find operations) but is markedly less precise — once two pointers are unified, all future information about either is shared, losing distinctions Andersen's analysis would preserve. It is the default choice when scalability on very large codebases matters more than precision.

**Type-based alias analysis (TBAA).** Rather than tracking points-to sets, TBAA infers non-aliasing from the source language's type system: under strict aliasing rules (ISO C/C++), an object of one type may not be legally accessed through an lvalue of an unrelated type (modulo `char*`/similar exceptions), so two memory accesses through incompatible types are assumed not to alias. LLVM encodes this via `!tbaa` metadata attached to load/store instructions, describing a type hierarchy; the alias analysis then answers may-alias queries cheaply by walking this metadata rather than doing points-to computation. This is unsound in the presence of type-punning violations, which is precisely why `-fno-strict-aliasing` exists as an escape hatch.

**LLVM's BasicAA and annotations.** LLVM's default alias analysis pass combines several lightweight, cheap heuristics rather than a single global algorithm: reasoning about `getelementptr` (GEP) offset arithmetic to prove two geps into the same object access disjoint ranges; recognizing "identified objects" (the result of `alloca`, `malloc`-like calls, or globals) that cannot alias distinct identified objects; and honoring explicit `noalias`/`restrict` parameter attributes and `noalias` metadata (often introduced by Polly or loop-vectorizer runtime checks) that assert disjointness contractually rather than by proof. Query results are classified as `MustAlias`, `MayAlias`, or `NoAlias` (with `PartialAlias` in some APIs), and this classification feeds directly into LICM legality, scheduling freedom, and vectorization legality (can two memory operations be reordered or packed into one vector op?).

**MemorySSA.** Built on top of a base alias analysis, MemorySSA is a sparse SSA-like representation of the *memory* program state: rather than tracking every load/store against every other, it introduces `MemoryDef`/`MemoryUse`/`MemoryPhi` nodes representing versions of "memory" analogous to how SSA tracks versions of scalar variables, letting optimizations like dead store elimination, LICM of loads, and redundancy elimination query memory dependencies in close-to-constant time via a dominator-tree walk rather than re-querying alias analysis pairwise.

## 3. Inlining

**Cost-based heuristic inlining.** Both GCC and LLVM use a threshold/benefit model: GCC's `inline-insns`-family parameters bound the estimated instruction-count growth from inlining a candidate; LLVM's `InlineCost` analysis walks the callee computing a weighted cost (accounting for instructions, calls, loops) offset by *bonuses* — notably a significant discount when actual call-site arguments are compile-time constants, since constant-propagation into the inlined body is likely to fold away branches and simplify further (modeled via a mini constant-folding simulation during cost estimation). The inliner accepts the call if the net cost is below a threshold that itself varies with optimization level and whether the call site is "hot" per profile data.

**Bottom-up SCC-ordered inlining.** Inlining decisions are made while traversing the call graph's strongly connected components (SCCs) typically bottom-up (callees before callers) so that by the time a caller is considered, its callees have already been fully optimized/inlined-into, giving accurate size/cost estimates. Recursive functions form single-node or multi-node SCCs that require special handling (bounded recursive inlining depth, or exclusion) since naive bottom-up processing doesn't terminate for self-recursive calls.

**Speculative devirtualization-driven inlining.** Indirect and virtual calls can't be inlined directly without knowing the target, but profile feedback (PGO) or inline-cache monitoring at a call site (HotSpot C2, Graal, V8 Turbofan) can identify a dominant monomorphic or polymorphic receiver type. The compiler then emits a *guarded inline*: a runtime type/class check followed by the inlined fast path for the predicted target and a fallback (deoptimization or a regular virtual call) otherwise. This is central to JIT performance on object-oriented workloads, converting the classic virtual-dispatch overhead into a branch plus inlined body in the common case.

**Partial inlining and LTO/ThinLTO.** Partial inlining duplicates only a function's "fast path" (e.g., a guard check and a short common case) into the caller while leaving a call to the cold remainder, reducing code growth versus full inlining while still eliminating call overhead on the hot path. Cross-module inlining is enabled by link-time optimization: classic LTO merges all translation units into one IR module before running the inliner, while ThinLTO instead generates per-module function *summaries* (approximate size/cost info) during compilation and performs cross-module import decisions using only those summaries plus on-demand function body import, preserving much of LTO's cross-module inlining benefit with far better scalability and parallelism.

## 4. Register Allocation

**Chaitin-Briggs graph-coloring allocation.** Builds an interference graph where nodes are live ranges (or, in SSA-based variants, SSA values) and edges connect live ranges simultaneously live at some program point. Register allocation becomes graph k-coloring (k = number of physical registers). The algorithm repeatedly *simplifies* by removing nodes with degree < k (pushing them on a stack, since they're guaranteed colorable), and when no such node exists, either spills a node (Chaitin's original *pessimistic* approach, choosing a spill candidate by a cost/degree heuristic) or, in Briggs's refinement, pushes a high-degree node onto the stack anyway *optimistically*, deferring the spill decision until the select phase actually fails to find a free color — since a high-degree node may still be colorable if its neighbors end up with fewer distinct colors than k. Coalescing (merging move-related nodes to eliminate copy instructions) is handled conservatively in Briggs's scheme (only coalescing nodes whose combined degree still permits simplification) versus the more aggressive Chaitin/George-Appel coalescing that risks reintroducing uncolorable nodes.

**Linear-scan register allocation (Poletto & Sarkar).** Instead of building an interference graph, live ranges are represented as intervals over a linearized instruction numbering, sorted by start point, and allocation proceeds by scanning these intervals in order, assigning free physical registers and evicting/spilling the interval with the furthest-away next use when registers run out. This sacrifices the precision of true interference-graph coloring (two live ranges that don't actually interfere at any shared program point but overlap in linear order may still be treated conservatively) for dramatically better compile-time complexity, making it the historical choice for low-latency JIT contexts — early LLVM had a "fast" linear-scan-like allocator, and early HotSpot client compiler (C1) used linear scan for quick tier-1 compilation.

**SSA-based optimal coloring via chordal graphs (Hack, Grund, Goos).** A key theoretical result: the interference graph of a program in SSA form is *chordal* (every cycle of length ≥ 4 has a chord), and chordal graphs can be optimally colored in polynomial time via a simplicial elimination ordering — no NP-hardness obstacle as in the general case. This enables allocators that exploit SSA structure directly for provably optimal register assignment (modulo spilling, which remains a separate, still-hard problem), influencing allocator design in SSA-centric compilers.

**LLVM's greedy register allocator.** A priority-based allocator operating on `LiveInterval`s (SSA-aware live ranges with sub-register and sub-range precision), processing live ranges in priority order (roughly, larger/more-used ranges first) and attempting direct assignment; on conflict, it may *evict* a lower-priority already-assigned interval back into the queue, or perform *live-range splitting* — dividing an interval at a program point so each piece can be allocated separately (splitting around a loop, at a basic-block boundary, or into local vs. global ranges) rather than spilling the whole value, with full spilling (inserting spill/reload code and rematerializing the value, i.e., recomputing it instead of reloading, when the defining instruction is cheap and side-effect-free) as the heuristic's fallback.

## 5. Escape Analysis

**Connection-graph-based escape analysis (Choi, Gupta, Serrano, Sreedhar, Midkiff).** Builds a connection graph relating object-creation sites, local references, and fields, propagating "escape state" through assignments, field stores, and calls. Objects are classified as `NoEscape` (never visible outside the allocating method/thread — eligible for stack allocation and lock elision), `ArgEscape` (passed to a callee but not stored anywhere persistent — may still permit some optimization but not stack allocation), or `GlobalEscape` (reachable from a static field, escaping thread, or return value — requires normal heap allocation). This classification underlies the classic interprocedural escape analysis used in IBM's Jikes RVM research and influenced HotSpot C2's own analysis.

**Scalar replacement and stack allocation from escape info.** When escape analysis proves an allocation `NoEscape`, the compiler can replace the heap object entirely with its constituent fields treated as independent scalar/SSA values (scalar replacement of aggregates), eliminating the allocation outright rather than merely relocating it, or at minimum allocate it on the stack frame. HotSpot C2 performs exactly this, additionally eliding synchronization (lock elision / avoiding the need for biased locking machinery) on monitors proven to guard only thread-local objects.

**Partial escape analysis with merge points (Graal).** Standard escape analysis is conservative at control-flow merges: if an object escapes on any path, it's treated as escaping everywhere. Graal's partial escape analysis instead tracks escape state per path and performs *materialization*: the object is kept virtual (scalar-replaced) along non-escaping paths and only actually allocated ("materialized") at the point where a path would cause it to escape, recovering scalar-replacement benefits even for conditionally-escaping objects that classic whole-method analysis would allocate eagerly.

**Precision limits.** Field-sensitivity (tracking escape per field rather than per object) and interprocedural depth both bound precision versus analysis cost; intraprocedural analyses are cheap but miss escapes/non-escapes visible only across call boundaries, while interprocedural analysis requires either whole-program visibility or conservative summaries at unanalyzable call boundaries (reflection, native calls), which is why JIT compilers (operating with full dynamic visibility at a call site) often achieve better escape precision in practice than static AOT compilers.

## 6. Instruction Scheduling

**List scheduling.** Builds a data dependence graph (DDG) per scheduling region (basic block or larger) encoding true/anti/output dependencies and modeling instruction latencies and functional-unit resource constraints; a priority function (commonly critical-path length from an instruction to the region's exit, i.e., an "as-late-as-possible" measure, or its dual "as-soon-as-possible" distance from entry) ranks ready instructions, and the scheduler greedily picks the highest-priority ready instruction at each cycle, respecting resource availability. This is the default scheduling approach in LLVM's `MachineScheduler` and GCC's Haifa scheduler.

**Modulo scheduling (Rau) for software pipelining.** Targets loops specifically: rather than scheduling one iteration at a time, it constructs a single steady-state schedule in which successive iterations overlap, with a new iteration initiated every *initiation interval* (II) cycles. The *minimum initiation interval* (MII) is a lower bound computed as the max of a resource-constrained MII (total resource demand per iteration divided by resource count) and a recurrence-constrained MII (cycle length of the tightest dependence recurrence divided by its distance), and the scheduler searches for a feasible schedule at increasing II starting from MII. This is the central scheduling technique for VLIW/EPIC architectures, notably Itanium, where ICC relies on modulo scheduling to fill the explicitly parallel instruction bundles.

**Trace scheduling (Fisher).** Extends scheduling beyond a single basic block by selecting a high-probability execution *trace* (a linear sequence of basic blocks along the expected hot path, chosen via profile data) and scheduling it as if it were one large block, hoisting and reordering instructions across the original block boundaries; because some control-flow exits leave the trace early or enter it mid-way, *compensation code* must be inserted on off-trace edges to preserve correctness for the paths not taken. This was developed for and is characteristic of early VLIW compilation.

**Sea-of-nodes scheduling.** IRs without an explicit block structure (HotSpot C2, V8 Turbofan) perform scheduling as a dedicated late compilation phase rather than relying on a pre-existing basic-block layout: a dual-pass approach computes an "early" placement (the earliest block a node could legally execute in, bounded by its dependencies, i.e., as-soon-as-possible) and a "late" placement (the latest legal block, bounded by uses, i.e., as-late-as-possible), then chooses a final placement within that range — commonly the shallowest-loop-nesting block within the range to avoid hoisting work into loops or sinking it unnecessarily — before finally running local list scheduling within each resulting basic block.

**Scheduling regions beyond basic blocks.** Superblocks (single-entry, multiple-exit regions formed by tail-duplicating code to eliminate side entrances) and hyperblocks (predicated/if-converted regions merging multiple control-flow paths into one predicated block) extend list scheduling's effective window, letting the scheduler move instructions across what were originally branch boundaries while preserving correctness via the duplication or predication that created the enlarged region.

## 7. Loop Vectorization

**Dependence analysis as a legality gate.** Before any loop can be vectorized, the compiler must prove no cross-iteration dependence is violated when iterations execute in SIMD-parallel groups. The GCD test checks whether an integer solution exists to the linear dependence equation derived from two array subscript expressions (a necessary but not sufficient condition — it can have false positives for dependence). Banerjee's test refines this using the actual loop bounds to test whether a real-valued solution exists within the iteration space's bounding box, giving better precision at polynomial cost. The Omega test solves the full integer linear programming formulation exactly, handling systems of constraints (multiple loops, multiple subscripts) at higher analysis cost — used when maximal precision is needed to vectorize or parallelize a non-trivially-indexed loop nest.

**SLP (superword-level parallelism) vectorization.** Distinct from loop vectorization: rather than vectorizing across loop iterations, Larsen & Amarasinghe's SLP algorithm finds *isomorphic* scalar operations within straight-line code (e.g., unrolled loop bodies, or independent scalar statements operating on adjacent array/struct elements) and packs them into a single vector instruction. LLVM's SLPVectorizer operates as a separate pass from the Loop Vectorizer, bottom-up building "vectorizable trees" from seed pairs of isomorphic, independent instructions and extending them through the use-def chains.

**Runtime legality checks (loop versioning).** When static alias/dependence analysis cannot prove absence of aliasing or overlap between pointers (common with pointer-based, non-array-subscript loops in C/C++), the vectorizer can emit a runtime memory-dependence check — comparing pointer ranges at the loop preheader — and generate two versions of the loop: a vectorized fast path guarded by the check, and a scalar fallback. LLVM's Loop Vectorizer does exactly this via its "memory runtime checks," along with separate alignment runtime checks when static alignment can't be proven.

**Reduction recognition.** Idioms like `sum += a[i]` or `max = max(max, a[i])` are recognized as *reductions* over an associative (and often commutative) operator; vectorizing them requires accumulating partial results in a vector register across iterations and then performing a horizontal reduction (a log-depth sequence of shuffles-and-adds, or a dedicated horizontal-add instruction) in an epilogue to combine the lanes into the scalar result, since the operator's associativity permits reordering but the final scalar value must still be produced correctly.

**If-conversion / predication.** Loops containing control flow (an `if` inside the loop body) can be vectorized by converting the conditional into a predicated/masked vector operation rather than a branch: each lane computes its result unconditionally but a per-lane mask (e.g., AVX-512 mask registers, or an explicit select/blend on architectures without mask registers) determines whether the result is committed, replacing control-flow divergence with data-parallel masking.

**Cost models driving VF/UF selection.** LLVM's VPlan-based vectorizer builds candidate vectorization plans at multiple vectorization factors (VF — how many loop iterations are packed per vector instruction) and interleave/unroll factors (UF — how many vector-width iterations are additionally unrolled to hide latency and improve instruction-level parallelism), evaluates each plan against a target-specific instruction cost table and register-pressure estimate, and selects the plan with the lowest estimated cost per element, since a higher VF is not always profitable (e.g., if it causes spilling or requires expensive shuffles for non-contiguous access patterns).

## 8. Loop Optimizations (Classical)

**Loop-invariant code motion (LICM).** Hoists computations whose operands don't change within the loop to the loop preheader. Correctness requires the hoisted computation to dominate all loop exits where its result is used (or, equivalently, that the original computation was *not* conditionally executed in a way that hoisting would newly execute it on paths where it previously wasn't) — speculative hoisting of a possibly-trapping operation (e.g., a division that might be by zero only on some iterations) is unsound unless the compiler can prove the operation can't fault, or sinks the computation only as far as legal.

**Induction variable recognition and strength reduction.** Identifies linear induction variables (variables incremented by a loop-invariant amount each iteration, expressible as `i = i0 + k*trip_count`) and rewrites derived expressions (e.g., array address computations like `base + i*4`) to use cheaper incremental updates instead of recomputing a multiplication each iteration — the classical Allen-Cocke-Kennedy/Cooper-Simpson-style strength-reduction algorithms normalize induction variables to a canonical form (a single normalized "canonical induction variable" counting 0, 1, 2, ...) from which all other induction variables are expressed as linear functions, simplifying both strength reduction and later bounds/overflow-check elimination.

**Loop unrolling and loop unswitching.** Full unrolling replicates the entire loop body for a statically-known trip count, eliminating loop-control overhead entirely; partial unrolling replicates the body a fixed factor and adjusts the loop increment/bound, trading code size for reduced branch overhead and improved scheduling freedom (more independent instructions available per iteration for the scheduler/vectorizer) — the unroll factor is typically chosen by a cost model balancing code growth against instruction-level-parallelism gain. Loop unswitching hoists a loop-invariant conditional (one whose condition doesn't change across iterations) out of the loop by duplicating the entire loop body into a then-branch and an else-branch, each containing a specialized (branch-free, in that dimension) copy of the loop — trading code duplication for eliminating a redundant per-iteration branch.

**Loop fusion, fission, and interchange.** Fusion merges two adjacent loops with compatible iteration spaces into one, improving locality and reducing loop overhead, legal only when no dependence would be violated by interleaving their bodies (checked via dependence analysis, generally requiring no dependence from the second loop's early iterations into the first loop's later ones). Fission/distribution is the inverse — splitting a loop body into multiple loops, useful for enabling vectorization of a sub-statement that's otherwise blocked by a dependence elsewhere in the same body. Loop interchange swaps the nesting order of two loops in a nest (e.g., to make the innermost loop stride contiguously through memory for better cache locality), legal exactly when the dependence direction vector for the nest does not have a "forward-then-backward" pattern that interchange would invert into an illegal backward dependence.

**Loop tiling / blocking.** Partitions a loop nest's iteration space into smaller blocks (tiles) sized to fit a cache level, reordering iteration so that all accesses to a tile's working set occur close together in time before moving to the next tile — dramatically improving reuse in cache-bound codes like dense matrix multiply, at the cost of more complex loop-control code (extra loop levels, boundary/remainder handling for non-divisible trip counts).

**Polyhedral optimization.** Represents each statement's iteration space as an integer polytope (a system of affine inequalities over loop indices and parameters) and expresses data accesses and the statement execution order as affine functions, enabling interchange, fusion, fission, tiling, and skewing to all be derived as a single affine *scheduling* transformation chosen to optimize a cost function (e.g., data locality or parallelism), rather than as separate pattern-matched legality checks per transformation. This unifying framework is implemented in GCC's Graphite and LLVM's Polly, both of which lower affine loop nests to a polyhedral model, run a scheduling algorithm (e.g., the Pluto algorithm), and regenerate optimized loop code — at the cost of being restricted to loops with affine bounds and affine array subscripts, falling back to simpler pairwise legality tests outside that scope.

---

Answer: The technical brief above covers all eight requested areas — SSA construction (dominance-frontier/Cytron et al. construction, Braun et al.'s incremental algorithm, SSA destruction with parallel-copy/φ-congruence handling), alias analysis (Andersen's inclusion-based analysis, Steensgaard's unification-based analysis, type-based alias analysis, LLVM's BasicAA heuristics, MemorySSA), register allocation (Chaitin-Briggs graph coloring, linear-scan allocation, SSA-based chordal-graph optimal coloring, LLVM's greedy allocator), inlining (cost-based heuristic inlining with constant-argument bonuses, SCC-ordered bottom-up inlining, speculative devirtualization/guarded inlining, partial inlining, LTO/ThinLTO cross-module inlining), escape analysis (connection-graph-based classification into NoEscape/ArgEscape/GlobalEscape, scalar replacement and lock elision from escape info, Graal's partial escape analysis with materialization), loop vectorization (dependence legality via GCD/Banerjee/Omega tests, SLP vectorization, runtime memory-dependence/alignment checks with loop versioning, reduction recognition, if-conversion/predication, VPlan-based cost-model-driven VF/UF selection), instruction scheduling (list scheduling with critical-path priority functions, Rau's modulo scheduling for software pipelining with MII computation, Fisher's trace scheduling with compensation code, sea-of-nodes early/late scheduling), and classical loop optimizations (LICM, induction variable strength reduction, unrolling and unswitching, fusion/fission/interchange, tiling, and the polyhedral model as implemented in Polly/Graphite) — each discussed with named algorithms, their underlying analyses, precision/complexity trade-offs, and real compiler implementations (LLVM, GCC, HotSpot C2, Graal, V8 Turbofan, Itanium ICC, Cranelift).

response.content:
# Technical Brief: Loop Vectorization and Classical Loop Optimizations

## 1. Loop Vectorization

### 1.1 Loop-level vectorization and dependence analysis prerequisites

Loop vectorization transforms a scalar loop iterating over array elements into a loop body that processes SIMD-width (VF) chunks per iteration using packed vector instructions (SSE/AVX/AVX-512 on x86, NEON/SVE on ARM). The transformation is a special case of unroll-and-pack: the iteration space `i = 0..N-1` is partitioned into strided blocks of size VF, and each scalar statement `S(i)` is replaced by a vector statement operating on `S(i), S(i+1), ..., S(i+VF-1)` simultaneously, with a scalar remainder loop (epilogue) handling the trip count modulo VF.

Legality hinges on absence of *loop-carried dependences* that would be violated by reordering or parallel execution of iterations within a vector. Three classical dependence tests, of increasing precision and cost, are used:

- **GCD test**: for array references with linear subscripts `a*i + b` in source and `c*i + d` in sink, a dependence can exist only if `gcd(a, c)` divides `(d - b)`. It is a necessary-not-sufficient test (yields false positives), O(1) per pair after linear subscript extraction, cheap but imprecise — it ignores loop bounds entirely.
- **Banerjee's test**: an inequality-based test that computes bounds on the dependence distance using the loop's iteration bounds, checking whether a real-valued solution exists within range. It is exact for single-index, single-loop affine cases but conservative (real relaxation of an integer problem) for multi-dimensional loop nests, trading soundness for tractable polynomial-time computation.
- **Omega test**: an exact integer linear programming-based test (Pugh) that decides dependence existence for systems of affine constraints over multiple loop indices, using the Omega test's variable-elimination procedure. It is precise but worst-case exponential, so production compilers apply it selectively (e.g., only after cheaper tests report "may-alias" or ambiguous results).

LLVM's `LoopAccessAnalysis` and GCC's `tree-data-ref.c` encode variants of these tests to classify data dependences by direction and distance vectors, determining whether a dependence is vectorization-safe (e.g., a distance ≥ VF in the same direction, or no dependence at all).

### 1.2 SLP (superword-level parallelism) vectorization

SLP vectorization, introduced by Larsen and Amarasinghe (PLDI 2000), is distinct from loop vectorization: rather than vectorizing across loop iterations, it finds *isomorphic* (structurally identical) scalar statements within a single basic block (or across unrolled iterations) and packs them into vector instructions. The canonical algorithm builds "packs" of isomorphic, independent scalar instructions (e.g., four independent scalar additions computing `c[0]=a[0]+b[0]`, `c[1]=a[1]+b[1]`, …), then performs a bottom-up or top-down traversal following the def-use graph to greedily combine candidate statements, inserting `shufflevector`/pack-unpack glue code at pack boundaries. LLVM's `SLPVectorizer` pass operates this way on straight-line code, often cooperating with the Loop Vectorizer: the Loop Vectorizer handles the cross-iteration parallelism while SLP handles within-iteration superword parallelism (e.g., vectorizing manually unrolled or structurally parallel code like RGB pixel processing or small matrix operations). GCC's `tree-vect-slp.c` implements an analogous "SLP tree" construction.

### 1.3 Vectorization legality/profitability analysis and runtime checks

Static dependence analysis is often inconclusive, particularly with pointer arguments lacking `restrict` qualification or with runtime-determined strides. LLVM's Loop Vectorizer addresses this via **loop versioning**: it generates a vectorized version guarded by runtime checks (memory-dependence runtime checks / pointer-disambiguation checks) that compare base pointers and strides to prove non-overlap for the specific execution, falling back to a scalar loop if the checks fail. This is implemented through `LoopVersioning` and `LoopAccessInfo`, producing SCEV-based (scalar evolution) bound checks. Overlap and alignment checks may be fused into a single runtime guard. ICC's auto-vectorizer historically used similar "vectorization with runtime data dependence testing," often paired with `#pragma ivdep`/`#pragma vector always` as programmer-asserted overrides when static proof is unavailable.

### 1.4 Reduction recognition

Associative/commutative reduction idioms (sum, product, min, max, bitwise AND/OR/XOR) are recognized via pattern matching on phi-nodes at the loop header: an accumulator phi combined with the loop body via one associative operator, with the phi's only external use being after the loop, identifies a *reduction variable*. Vectorizing a reduction requires accumulating VF partial sums in a vector register across iterations, then emitting a **horizontal reduction epilogue** (a tree of `shufflevector`+`add` operations, or a single hardware horizontal-add/`vpsadbw`/`vphadd`-style instruction, or LLVM's `llvm.vector.reduce.*` intrinsics lowered to target-specific reduction sequences). Because floating-point addition is not strictly associative, reassociation requires `-ffast-math` or explicit `#pragma omp simd reduction`/fast-math flags to permit reordering; GCC and LLVM both gate FP reduction vectorization behind relaxed FP contraction flags unless the reduction is integer.

### 1.5 If-conversion / predication

Loops containing control flow (if/else inside the loop body) are vectorized via **if-conversion**: branches are converted into straight-line code using select/masked instructions, so each lane of the vector computes its own result and a predicate mask determines which lanes commit their result. On AVX-512 and ARM SVE, explicit mask registers (`k0`-`k7` on AVX-512) allow masked loads/stores/arithmetic, avoiding the need for blend-based merging. LLVM's `VPlan` constructs explicit `VPBlendRecipe`/`VPWidenSelectRecipe` nodes during if-conversion within the Loop Vectorizer; GCC's tree-level if-conversion pass (`tree-if-conv.c`) runs as a preparatory pass before the vectorizer.

### 1.6 Vectorization cost models, VF/UF selection, VPlan

Choosing the vectorization factor (VF) and interleave/unroll factor (UF) is a profitability decision driven by a **cost model**: per-instruction cost tables (latency/throughput for each vector width on the target microarchitecture), scalarization cost for operations lacking vector support, and register pressure estimation to avoid spilling. LLVM's Loop Vectorizer builds multiple candidate `VPlan`s (Vectorization Plan, a target-independent IR for candidate vectorized loop versions) for different VF/UF combinations, evaluates each via `LoopVectorizationCostModel`, and selects the plan minimizing estimated cost per element while respecting register-file constraints. GCC's vectorizer performs an analogous cost comparison using `targetm.vectorize.builtin_vectorization_cost`.

---

## 2. Classical (Non-Vectorization) Loop Optimizations

### 2.1 Loop-invariant code motion (LICM)

LICM hoists computations whose operands do not change across loop iterations out of the loop body into the preheader, reducing redundant work. A candidate instruction `I` is loop-invariant if all its operands are either defined outside the loop or are themselves loop-invariant (computed via a fixed-point dataflow over the loop body). Hoisting is legal only if additional preconditions hold: the hoisted point (the preheader) must dominate all uses of `I` inside the loop, and **the loop must execute at least once, or hoisting must be speculation-safe** — i.e., `I` must not have side effects (no memory stores, no trapping behavior such as division-by-zero or faulting loads) unless the compiler can prove the original instruction always executes (guarded by `isGuaranteedToExecute`), since otherwise introducing it unconditionally into the preheader could trigger undefined behavior (a trap) on a path where the original loop body would have exited before reaching `I`. LLVM's `LICM` pass performs this at the LLVM IR level, cooperating with `MemorySSA` to additionally hoist/sink loads and stores when it can prove no aliasing stores occur in the loop (store motion/scalar promotion of memory). GCC's equivalent is the `tree-ssa-loop-im.c` invariant motion pass, operating on GIMPLE with similar dominance and trap-safety preconditions.

### 2.2 Induction variable recognition and strength reduction

An induction variable (IV) is a variable whose value in each iteration is an affine function of the iteration count (`i*c + d` for linear IVs; higher-degree/"chain of recurrences" variables are polynomial). Compilers normalize induction variables into a canonical form (a single "canonical" IV counting `0, 1, 2, ...`, with other IVs expressed in terms of it via SCEV — scalar evolution — in LLVM, or `chrec` — chains of recurrences — in GCC). **Strength reduction** replaces expensive operations derived from an IV (e.g., array-address computation via multiplication `base + i*stride`) with cheaper incremental updates (`addr += stride` each iteration), eliminating multiplications inside the loop. The classical algorithm is **Cooper, Simpson, and Vick's "SSA-based strength reduction"** (an evolution of the original Allen-Cocke-Kennedy strength reduction algorithm from the 1970s PTRAN/parallelizing-compiler literature), which operates over the SSA representation of derived induction variables, identifying "IV families" linearly related to a base IV and rewriting them with cheaper recurrence updates. LLVM implements this in `IndVarSimplify` (canonicalization) and `LoopStrengthReduce` (candidate formula generation and cost-based selection among competing strength-reduced forms, considering target addressing modes). GCC's `tree-ssa-loop-ivopt.c` performs analogous IV optimization with explicit cost modeling for addressing-mode fit.

### 2.3 Loop unrolling and loop unswitching

**Loop unrolling** replicates the loop body K times (the unroll factor) per iteration of the control variable, reducing loop-overhead (branch and increment instructions) per unit of work and exposing more instruction-level parallelism and scheduling freedom to the backend. *Full unrolling* eliminates the loop entirely when the trip count is a compile-time constant; *partial unrolling* replicates by a chosen factor and retains a trailing loop (or remainder handling) for the non-multiple iterations. Unroll factor selection is a profitability trade-off balancing code-size growth (I-cache pressure), register pressure from overlapping live ranges of replicated bodies, and reduced loop-control overhead; LLVM's `LoopUnroll` pass uses a cost model (instruction count threshold, partial-unroll heuristics keyed to estimated benefit from exposed ILP) and may act on explicit `#pragma unroll`/`#pragma clang loop unroll_count` hints. **Loop unswitching** hoists a loop-invariant conditional (a branch whose condition does not change across iterations) outside the loop by duplicating the loop body into two versions, one per branch outcome, eliminating the repeated per-iteration branch test at the cost of code duplication. LLVM's `LoopUnswitch`/`SimpleLoopUnswitch` pass implements this, bounded by a duplication-cost threshold to avoid exponential code blowup when multiple invariant conditions are nested.

### 2.4 Loop fusion and loop fission/distribution

**Loop fusion** merges two adjacent loops with compatible iteration spaces into a single loop body, improving data locality (shared array accesses amortize cache line fetches) and reducing loop-overhead instruction count. Legality requires that no dependence exists between the second loop's reads/writes and the first loop's writes that would be reordered illegally by fusion — formally, fusion is legal if there is no dependence from a statement in loop 2 to a statement in loop 1 that would, after fusion, execute in the wrong relative order (checked via the same dependence/direction-vector machinery used for vectorization). **Loop fission (distribution)** is the inverse: splitting one loop into multiple loops over disjoint subsets of its statements, useful for isolating a vectorizable portion of a loop body from a non-vectorizable portion (e.g., splitting out a statement containing a function call with side effects), or for breaking a cyclic dependence into separate loops with partial-order execution. GCC's `tree-loop-distribution.c` performs fission explicitly to enable subsequent vectorization or memset/memcpy pattern recognition; LLVM has an explicit `LoopDistribute` pass for similar purposes, driven by the same `LoopAccessAnalysis` dependence information.

### 2.5 Loop interchange

Loop interchange swaps the nesting order of two loops in a loop nest (e.g., converting row-major to column-major traversal) to improve spatial locality by making the innermost loop's stride match the array's memory layout, improving cache-line reuse and enabling subsequent vectorization of the (now contiguous-stride) innermost loop. Legality requires proof via the **dependence direction vector**: for each dependence between statements in the nest, the direction vector entry (`<`, `=`, `>`) for each loop level must remain lexicographically non-reversed after the proposed interchange — concretely, interchange is illegal if it would cause a dependence with direction `<` at the interchanged level to become inconsistent with execution order. This is checked via the same Banerjee/Omega-test machinery producing distance/direction vectors per loop level. GCC's `graphite` infrastructure and LLVM's `LoopInterchange` pass both implement legality checks over direction-vector matrices before applying the transform, with profitability driven by estimated cache-miss reduction (often using a simplified cost model based on reuse distance).

### 2.6 Loop tiling/blocking for cache locality

Tiling (blocking) partitions the iteration space of a loop nest into smaller rectangular (or more generally, polyhedral) blocks sized to fit a target cache level's capacity, reordering execution to complete all work within a tile before moving to the next, maximizing data reuse within the cache and reducing capacity misses. This requires the same legality precondition as interchange/fusion — the dependence structure must permit the chosen tile traversal order — and introduces additional loop levels (tile loops wrapping point loops). Tile size selection is typically a cost-model/heuristic decision based on target cache size, associativity, and working-set estimates, sometimes autotuned. GCC's Graphite and LLVM's Polly both implement tiling as a schedule transformation within their respective polyhedral frameworks rather than as an ad hoc pattern-matched pass.

### 2.7 Polyhedral loop optimization framework

The polyhedral model represents each statement instance in a loop nest as an integer point in an **iteration-space polytope** defined by affine inequality constraints derived from loop bounds and conditionals (requiring that bounds, array subscripts, and dependencies are affine functions of enclosing loop indices and parameters — the Static Control Part, or SCoP, restriction). Data dependences are represented as affine relations between polytope points, and the compiler computes a new **affine schedule** (a function mapping each statement instance to a new execution timestamp/multidimensional time vector) that is legal (respects all dependence constraints) and optimized for a target objective (locality, parallelism, tiling feasibility) — commonly via the Pluto algorithm's affine scheduling formulation solved by integer linear programming, or via the Feautrier scheduling algorithm which maximizes degree of parallelism under lexicographic legality constraints. This unifies interchange, fusion, fission, skewing, and tiling as different instances of schedule selection within one algebraic framework rather than as independently pattern-matched transformations, at the cost of being restricted to SCoPs and incurring ILP-solving overhead. **Graphite** is GCC's polyhedral framework (built on ISL — the Integer Set Library — for polyhedral computation), and **Polly** is LLVM's analogous framework (also built on ISL), both performing SCoP detection, dependence-polyhedra construction, schedule optimization (often invoking the Pluto algorithm via ISL's scheduler), and code generation (quasi-affine loop bound regeneration, "polyhedral AST generation") back into the compiler's IR.

response.content:
# Technical Brief: SSA Construction, Alias Analysis, and Inlining

## 1. SSA Construction

**Dominance-frontier construction (Cytron, Ferrante, Rosen, Wegman, Zadeck 1991).** The CFRWZ algorithm is the canonical method for placing φ-nodes to build minimal SSA form. It proceeds in two phases. First, compute the dominator tree of the CFG (via Lengauer-Tarjan or the simpler iterative Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy algorithm). Node A dominates B if every path from entry to B passes through A. The dominance frontier of a node N, DF(N), is the set of nodes B such that N dominates a predecessor of B but N does not strictly dominate B itself — intuitively, the frontier marks where N's dominance "runs out" and control-flow merges happen. Second, for each variable v, compute the iterated dominance frontier (IDF) of the set of blocks assigning v: DF⁺ = DF ∪ DF(DF) ∪ ... until fixpoint. A φ-node for v is inserted at every block in DF⁺(defs(v)). After placement, a renaming pass walks the dominator tree, maintaining a per-variable stack of current SSA names, pushing a fresh name at each definition (including φ-node outputs) and popping on exit from the dominator subtree. This produces minimal SSA: exactly one φ per join point per variable with multiple reaching definitions, no more. Complexity is near-linear in practice (dominance frontier sizes are bounded in real CFGs), though worst-case frontier size is quadratic.

**Minimal vs. pruned SSA and sparse construction.** Minimal SSA, as produced directly by CFRWZ, can still contain φ-nodes for variables that are not live past the merge point — dead φs. Pruned SSA eliminates these by consulting liveness information before or during insertion: a φ for variable v is only inserted at a block B if v is live-in at B. This requires a liveness analysis pass (or a combined live-variables/SSA construction) but yields a strictly smaller SSA graph, which matters for sparse dataflow algorithms (sparse conditional constant propagation, SSAPRE) whose cost scales with the number of SSA values rather than program points. GCC's GIMPLE SSA form historically computes pruned SSA for this reason, tracking `SSA_NAME` liveness via its `tree-ssa` infrastructure. The distinction is purely about eliminating unnecessary φs; both forms are still in "SSA form" in the dominance-frontier sense.

**Braun et al. (2013) — simple and efficient SSA construction.** This algorithm avoids computing dominance frontiers at all, instead constructing SSA directly during a single forward pass over the CFG as it is being built (e.g., while parsing), using local value numbering per basic block. Each block maintains a map from variable to current SSA value. A read of variable v in block B first checks B's local map; if absent, `readVariableRecursive` is invoked: if B has exactly one predecessor, the value is read recursively from that predecessor (no φ needed); if B has multiple predecessors, a φ-node is optimistically created, recorded as B's current definition for v (to break infinite recursion on loops), and then its operands are filled in by recursively reading v from each predecessor. The key innovation handling forward construction before all predecessors are known is the **sealed/unsealed block** distinction: a block is "unsealed" if not all of its predecessors have yet been added to the CFG (common when processing loop headers before the loop body is parsed). For unsealed blocks, an **incomplete φ-node** is created with blank operand slots; the block is placed on a worklist and "sealed" (operands finalized) once all predecessors are known. After construction, a simplification pass removes **trivial φ-nodes**: a φ with all non-self operands equal (or a φ with only one distinct operand) is replaced by that operand, recursively re-triggering simplification on φs that used it — this is essentially an inlined form of global value numbering and naturally prunes redundant φs without a separate dominance-frontier pass, converging to minimal (though not always pruned) SSA. This technique is attractive for JIT and single-pass or streaming compilers because it has no separate dominator-tree computation phase; it is used in Cranelift's frontend (cranelift-frontend's `SSABuilder`) and conceptually similar lazy approaches appear in various LLVM-frontend code generators (e.g., some `clang`-adjacent and educational LLVM frontends use it to avoid building explicit CFG dominance info before SSA).

**Sea-of-Nodes as an alternative.** Rather than CFG + explicit SSA with φ-nodes at merges, the sea-of-nodes IR (used in HotSpot C2, Graal, and V8 TurboFan) represents control and data dependencies uniformly as a graph with no fixed total order; control-flow merges are represented by explicit `Merge`/`Region` nodes and φ-equivalents are `Phi` nodes attached to those regions, while nodes with no control dependency "float" and are scheduled late. This is not a different SSA theory but a different IR organization that makes SSA's def-use structure the primary representation rather than CFG-plus-annotation, simplifying some optimizations (global code motion, GVN) at the cost of a more complex late scheduling pass to reconstruct a linear order before codegen.

**SSA destruction.** Converting back to non-SSA (register-machine) code requires eliminating φ-nodes, conceptually by replacing each φ at a join with a **parallel copy** at the end of each predecessor block (all source-to-destination copies in a parallel copy execute simultaneously, reading all sources before writing any destination). Naively sequentializing parallel copies is unsound in general: the **lost-copy problem** arises when a value needed by a later copy is overwritten by an earlier one, and the **swap problem** arises with cyclic dependencies (e.g., a φ resulting in the moves a←b, b←a, which requires a temporary or an actual swap, not a sequential copy). The standard solution (Sreedhar et al., and refined by Boissinot et al. "Revisiting Out-of-SSA Translation") builds a dependency graph of the parallel copy, detects cycles, and sequentializes using a temporary register to break cycles. A separate, more global technique groups SSA values connected transitively by φ-node operands into **φ-congruence classes**; if all members of a class can be assigned the same physical location, the φ (and its copies) can be eliminated entirely rather than materialized as a copy — this is where SSA destruction integrates with **register coalescing** in the register allocator. LLVM performs SSA destruction in its register allocation pipeline (`PHIElimination` pass converts φs into copies in predecessor blocks before `VirtRegRewriter`/coalescing), and GCC's GIMPLE-to-RTL lowering (`out-of-ssa`) performs analogous coalescing-aware copy insertion via `tree-outof-ssa.cc`.

---

## 2. Alias Analysis

**Andersen's analysis.** This is an inclusion-based (subset-constraint) points-to analysis. For each pointer variable p, Andersen's computes a points-to set pts(p) ⊆ Objects, and constraints from assignments generate subset relations: `p = q` yields pts(q) ⊆ pts(p); `p = &a` yields a ∈ pts(p); `p = *q` and `*p = q` yield conditional subset constraints dereferencing through points-to sets. The algorithm is a fixpoint iteration over these inclusion constraints (naively cubic, O(n³), because each of n variables can have up to n objects in its points-to set, and constraint propagation can require revisiting on each growth — practical implementations use difference propagation and worklist algorithms, e.g., Pearce/Hendren/Verbrugge's "Ant"/"Bear"-style solvers, or BDD-based encodings as in `bddbddb`, to make it scale). Andersen's is flow-insensitive (one points-to set per variable for the whole program, ignoring program order) and typically context-insensitive in its base form, but it is more precise than Steensgaard's because subset relations are directional rather than collapsed.

**Steensgaard's analysis.** This is a unification-based points-to analysis: instead of subset constraints, assignment `p = q` causes the points-to sets (really, the abstract storage locations / "ECR" — equivalence class representative — nodes) of p and q to be *unified* into one equivalence class via a union-find structure. This loses direction (p and q become aliases of exactly the same future points-to information even though real aliasing is asymmetric), giving substantially lower precision but near-linear time complexity, O(n·α(n)) with union-find's near-constant amortized operations. Steensgaard's is the standard answer when "almost-linear" whole-program points-to information is needed, e.g., certain GCC alias-analysis prototypes and early whole-program analyses prioritizing scalability over precision.

**Type-based alias analysis (TBAA).** TBAA infers non-aliasing from the source language's type system rather than from pointer-flow constraints. Under C/C++ strict aliasing rules, an object of type T may only be accessed through an lvalue of a compatible type (T, a signed/unsigned variant, char, or an aggregate containing T); accesses through unrelated types are undefined behavior, which the compiler exploits to assume no-alias between differently-typed accesses. LLVM implements this via `!tbaa` metadata attached to load/store instructions encoding a type hierarchy (a DAG of "access tags" including struct-path info for field-sensitivity, i.e., "struct-path TBAA"), and a corresponding `TypeBasedAliasAnalysis` pass answers alias queries by walking the type hierarchy for compatibility. This is unsound under `-fno-strict-aliasing` and is a frequent source of real-world miscompilation bug reports when C code violates strict aliasing (e.g., type-punning through unions without using `memcpy` or compiler-recognized idioms).

**Flow-sensitivity and context-sensitivity.** Flow-sensitive analyses compute distinct points-to/alias facts at each program point, tracking kills and strong updates (precise but expensive, usually limited to intraprocedural or restricted scopes); flow-insensitive analyses (Andersen's, Steensgaard's base forms) compute one global summary ignoring statement order, which is sound only with weak updates (union, never kill) but scales to whole programs. Orthogonally, context-sensitive analyses distinguish different call sites/call paths of the same function (e.g., via call-strings, k-CFA, or BDD-represented context cloning), while context-insensitive analyses merge all calls to a function into one summary, risking false aliasing across unrelated call sites but avoiding exponential blowup.

**LLVM BasicAA.** LLVM's default, cheap, intraprocedural alias analysis is `BasicAAResult` (BasicAA pass). It uses several non-exhaustive heuristics rather than a full points-to solve: (1) **identified-object** reasoning — allocas, globals, and noalias-returning calls (malloc-like) are treated as provably-distinct base objects unless they can be shown to escape and alias; (2) **GEP-based offset reasoning** — for two `getelementptr` expressions off the same base pointer, BasicAA symbolically decomposes the offset into a constant part and a sum of variable*scale terms, and if the offsets are provably disjoint given the access sizes, the memory accesses are declared `NoAlias`; (3) explicit **`noalias`/`restrict`** parameter and return attributes, propagated from C's `restrict` qualifier or Rust's unique-reference guarantees, which BasicAA and dependent passes trust directly without re-deriving. BasicAA composes with other AA implementations (TBAA, `scoped-noalias`, CFL-AA) through LLVM's `AAResults` aggregator, which queries each in turn and takes the most precise answer.

**Alias classification and its consumers.** Every alias query resolves to one of `MustAlias` (always the same memory location), `MayAlias` (unknown/conservative), `NoAlias` (provably disjoint), or `PartialAlias` (overlapping but not identical). This classification directly gates legality of instruction scheduling (two stores that MayAlias cannot be reordered), LICM (a load cannot be hoisted out of a loop past a store that MayAlias it), and vectorization (SLP/loop vectorizers must prove NoAlias, often via runtime bounds checks when static alias analysis is inconclusive — LLVM's loop vectorizer inserts "memory runtime checks" in exactly this situation).

**MemorySSA.** LLVM's `MemorySSA` is a sparse SSA-like representation of the *memory state* rather than scalar values, built on top of an underlying alias analysis. It defines `MemoryDef` (a store/clobbering access), `MemoryUse` (a read, linked to the nearest dominating clobbering def via alias queries), and `MemoryPhi` (merging memory states at CFG joins, placed using the same dominance-frontier machinery as scalar SSA). Because MemoryUse nodes skip over non-aliasing MemoryDefs (using the AA oracle to walk back through the def chain), MemorySSA gives a sparse, directly-indexable chain of "which store last touched memory I might overlap with," avoiding the need to conservatively treat every store as potentially clobbering every load. It underlies GVN-based load elimination, DSE (dead store elimination), and LICM's memory-dependence queries in modern LLVM, replacing the older, coarser `MemoryDependenceAnalysis` in many of these passes.

---

## 3. Inlining

**Cost-based heuristic inlining.** The baseline mechanism in essentially every production compiler is a threshold-driven cost/benefit model applied at each call site. GCC's inliner (`ipa-inline`) computes an estimated instruction-count growth for the caller against limits such as `-finline-insns-single`/`-finline-insns-auto` and a global `--param inline-unit-growth`, using IPA (interprocedural analysis) summaries of callee size computed once in GIMPLE. LLVM's `InlineCost` analysis (`llvm/Analysis/InlineCost.cpp`) walks the callee's IR estimating a weighted size cost (per-instruction costs, with special-cased cheap instructions) against a `DefaultThreshold`/`OptMinSizeThreshold`/`HotCallSiteThreshold` tuned by optimization level and PGO hotness, and nets out a **bonus/discount model**: if an argument at the call site is a constant, LLVM partially constant-folds/simplifies the callee body during the cost walk (`InstructionsSimplified` discount) to detect that inlining would enable significant downstream simplification (dead branch elimination, etc.), discounting the effective cost accordingly — this is the call-site-specific "threshold adjusted by constant-argument folding" mechanism. A call is inlined only if estimated cost ≤ threshold.

**Bottom-up vs. top-down order and SCC processing.** Inlining decisions are order-dependent: inlining callees before deciding about their own callers (bottom-up) lets the inliner reason about a callee's *final*, already-inlined size, while top-down order processes outer callers first. Both LLVM's legacy and new (SCC-pass-manager-based) inliners process the call graph's **strongly connected components** in reverse topological (bottom-up) order using Tarjan's SCC algorithm on the call graph: a non-recursive leaf function is inlined into its callers first, so that by the time a caller is itself considered as an inlining candidate, its body already reflects prior inlining. Recursive functions form a nontrivial SCC (self-loops or mutual recursion); compilers special-case these — typically inlining a bounded number of levels of self-recursion (or none) to avoid unbounded code growth, since a naive bottom-up visit cannot "finish" an SCC the way it finishes a DAG node.

**Speculative devirtualization.** For indirect/virtual calls, static inlining is blocked unless the callee can be proven unique. JIT compilers instead inline speculatively using runtime profile feedback: HotSpot's C2 compiler uses **CHA (class hierarchy analysis)** to check whether a virtual call site currently has only one implementing subclass loaded, enabling direct "monomorphic" inlining guarded by a cheap class/`CompiledIC` check with a deoptimization fallback if a new subclass is later loaded; when CHA cannot prove uniqueness, C2 and Graal use **inline caches** and type-profile feedback collected by the interpreter/baseline tier to insert a guarded, explicit type check (`if (obj.getClass() == ExpectedClass) inlined-body else slow-path-call`) — "polymorphic inlining" handles the top 2 profiled types with a cascade of guards. V8's TurboFan performs the analogous transformation using feedback vectors recorded by Ignition (its interpreter) to speculatively inline megamorphic/polymorphic call sites behind `CheckMaps`-style guards, bailing to deopt on a map mismatch. These are all instances of **guarded inlining**: correctness is preserved by inserting a cheap runtime check and a slow/deopt path rather than by static proof.

**Partial inlining.** Rather than inlining an entire callee, partial inlining extracts a "hot" subset of the callee's control flow (often a fast-path early-return guarded by a simple condition) and inlines only that fragment at the call site, leaving a call to the (outlined) remainder for the cold path. LLVM's `PartialInlinerLegacyPass`/`partial-inliner` performs exactly this: it identifies single-entry/single-exit regions that dominate an early return and outlines the rest into a separate function, inlining only the cheap prefix. This targets the common case where a function's size is dominated by a rarely-executed slow path.

**Metadata/alias-set duplication and EH interaction.** Inlining physically copies IR, which raises two correctness-adjacent bookkeeping problems. First, `noalias`/`restrict` scoped-metadata (LLVM's "noalias scope" `llvm.loop`/`!alias.scope` and `!noalias` metadata attached to the callee) must be **cloned with fresh, uniquified scope identifiers per call site** when a function is inlined at multiple call sites; failing to do so would make unrelated call sites appear to share a noalias domain, causing either missed optimizations or (if done incorrectly) unsound aliasing assumptions leaking across call sites. LLVM's inliner explicitly remaps `!alias.scope`/`!noalias` metadata through a fresh `MDNode` domain per inlined instance for this reason. Second, inlining a callee that contains exception-handling constructs (try/catch, landing pads) into a caller requires duplicating and relinking **EH tables** — the callee's landing-pad/personality-routine linkage, and especially its unwind-destination edges, must be rewritten to point into the caller's exception-handling structure (e.g., LLVM must correctly nest/merge `invoke`/`landingpad` chains, and cloning a callee's EH regions multiple times at multiple call sites multiplies the number of landing pads and associated LSDA table entries, an often underappreciated code-size cost of inlining functions with non-trivial EH).

**Whole-program / link-time inlining.** Ordinary inlining is bounded by what the compiler can see in a single translation unit. LTO (link-time optimization, as in LLVM's monolithic "full LTO," which merges all translation units' IR into one module before running standard IPA/inlining passes) and **ThinLTO** both extend inlining across translation-unit boundaries. ThinLTO avoids full-module merging by instead emitting a **function summary** per translation unit during the compile step (a lightweight description of each function's size/cost, call edges, and whether it's a candidate for cross-module inlining), then performing a fast whole-program analysis over just these summaries at link time to decide which functions should be **imported** (their IR cloned) into other modules before each module is optimized independently and in parallel. This gives most of full LTO's cross-module inlining benefit with far better build-time scalability, and is the mechanism behind Clang/LLVM's `-flto=thin`; GCC's analogous WHOPR (Whole Program Optimization via partitioning) IPA-LTO mode performs a similar summary-based cross-partition inlining/cloning step at `-flto`.

# Technical Brief: Register Allocation, Escape Analysis, Instruction Scheduling

## 1. Register Allocation

**Graph-coloring register allocation (Chaitin-Briggs).** The classical formulation (Chaitin et al., 1981; refined by Briggs, Cooper, Torczon, 1994) models allocation as graph coloring. Liveness analysis produces live ranges (webs); an interference graph is built with one node per live range and an edge between two ranges that are simultaneously live at some program point (derived from live-out sets at each instruction, conservatively using live-variable analysis rather than exact live ranges in the original Chaitin formulation). A k-coloring of this graph, where k is the number of physical registers in a given class, corresponds to a valid assignment. Chaitin's algorithm uses a **simplify/spill/select worklist**: repeatedly remove ("simplify") nodes of degree < k and push them on a stack, since such nodes are guaranteed colorable regardless of their neighbors' colors; when no such node exists, a node is chosen to **spill** (insert loads/stores around uses/defs and remove it from the graph) using a spill cost heuristic (typically estimated spill cost / degree, weighted by loop nesting depth); after reduction, nodes are popped and assigned the lowest-numbered color not used by already-colored neighbors ("select"). Chaitin's original algorithm spills pessimistically — any node picked for spill during simplification is spilled unconditionally even if, when popped later, a color happens to be free. **Briggs' optimistic coloring** fixes this: potential-spill nodes are still pushed onto the stack (not immediately rewritten with spill code), and only during the select phase, if no color is actually available, is the node marked an actual spill. This recovers many spills that pessimistic Chaitin would have incurred.

Coalescing merges move-related live ranges (typically from copies inserted by SSA destruction or calling-convention fixups) to eliminate the move, but naive coalescing can increase the merged node's degree and induce spills. **Briggs-style conservative coalescing** merges two nodes only if the resulting merged node has fewer than k neighbors of degree ≥ k (a safe, degree-bounded test), guaranteeing colorability is preserved. **Chaitin/George-Appel aggressive coalescing** instead coalesces whenever the merged node's neighbor set is a subset of the union of each node's neighbors meeting a more permissive safety test (George & Appel's criterion: for each neighbor t of a, either t already interferes with b or t has degree < k), coalescing more pairs but risking additional spills, usually mitigated by iterating coalescing and simplification (iterated register coalescing, George & Appel 1996) and by biased coloring/optimistic rollback.

**Linear-scan register allocation (Poletto & Sarkar, 1999).** Rather than building an explicit interference graph, each variable's live range is approximated by a single contiguous **live interval** [start, end] over a linearized instruction numbering (assuming values don't have holes, or handling holes via split intervals). Live intervals are sorted by start point and scanned left to right; active intervals are kept in a set ordered by end point. When a new interval begins, if a free physical register exists it's assigned; otherwise the active interval with the furthest end point is spilled (or the new one is spilled), under the heuristic that spilling the longest remaining interval frees the most future register pressure. This runs in near-linear time (O(n log n) with interval trees/sorted structures) versus the higher polynomial/potentially superlinear cost of graph-coloring's interference-graph construction and iterative worklist, trading allocation quality for speed. It was used in early **HotSpot's client compiler (C1)** and the original **LLVM "fast" register allocator** (and historically linear scan was LLVM's primary allocator before "greedy" replaced it as default), both contexts where JIT compile-time latency dominates over maximal code quality.

**SSA-based / chordal-graph optimal coloring (Hack, Grund, Goos).** A key theoretical result: the interference graph of a program in strict SSA form, when each live range is a single SSA value, is **chordal** (every cycle of length ≥ 4 has a chord), because SSA liveness follows a tree-like dominance structure. Chordal graphs are colorable optimally in polynomial time via **perfect elimination orderings** (simplicial elimination), so the NP-hard general coloring problem's hardness is sidestepped entirely for SSA-form interference graphs — simplify never needs heuristic choice among multiple degree-<k candidates in the way that matters for optimality, and coloring is exact given a fixed register budget (ignoring spilling, which remains a separate, still heuristic, decision). This underlies "puzzle solving" allocators that decouple spilling (done first, as a separate NP-hard problem addressed heuristically) from coloring (done exactly afterward on the now-colorable SSA graph), and requires explicit SSA destruction afterward to resolve phi-nodes into real moves/registers.

**LLVM's "greedy" register allocator.** LLVM's default (post-linear-scan) allocator is priority-based: live ranges are represented as `LiveInterval` objects (interval lists with interval trees for efficient overlap queries), ordered in a priority queue by size/spill weight/loop depth. The algorithm repeatedly pops the highest-priority unallocated range and attempts physical-register assignment; if no register is free it considers **eviction** of a lower-priority range already assigned (if the evicted range's priority is lower, triggering a requeue of the evicted range), or **live-range splitting** — breaking the range into smaller pieces (region splitting at loop boundaries, local splitting within a block) so each piece individually fits available registers, deferring spill code insertion until splitting options are exhausted. True "spill everywhere" (inserting loads/stores at every use/def of a range) is the last resort, since splitting generally produces cheaper code (fewer total load/store insertions) by spilling only across the long portions of a range, not every access.

**Spilling vs. rematerialization.** Instead of spilling a value to the stack and reloading it, **rematerialization** recomputes the value from cheaper, already-available operands (e.g., reloading a constant or re-executing a cheap address computation) at the use point, avoiding memory traffic entirely when the recomputation cost is lower than a spill/reload pair; Chaitin-Briggs and LLVM's greedy allocator both support rematerialization as an alternative spill-cost choice, driven by per-value "rematerializable" flags set during instruction selection.

**Coalescing and SSA destruction.** Phi-nodes define **phi-congruence classes** — sets of SSA values (the phi result and its operands) that ideally should be assigned the same physical location so the phi can be eliminated as a no-op rather than realized as copies. SSA destruction algorithms (e.g., Sreedhar et al.'s phi-congruence-based translation, or Boissinot et al.'s simpler "coalescing out of SSA") attempt to coalesce all members of a congruence class into one live range where interference permits, falling back to copy insertion (parallel copies lowered to sequential moves respecting swap semantics) where values genuinely interfere.

## 2. Escape Analysis

**Connection-graph-based escape analysis (Choi, Gupta, Serrano, Sreedhar, Midkiff — IBM, 1999/2003).** This algorithm builds a **connection graph** per method: nodes represent objects (abstracted by allocation site) and references/fields; edges represent points-to and field-points-to relationships, with special "phantom" nodes representing unknown external objects that callers/callees might reference. Each object node is classified into one of three escape states, forming a lattice from most to least restrictive: **NoEscape** (the object is accessible only within the current method/thread and never escapes, including not passed to callees in a way that lets them stash it outside), **ArgEscape** (the object escapes via being passed as an argument or returned, reachable by the callee or caller, but not provably escaping to another thread or the heap globally), and **GlobalEscape** (the object may be reachable by another thread or stored into a static/heap-escaping location, the least precise, most conservative classification). The analysis propagates escape states along connection-graph edges (an object connected to a GlobalEscape object is at least ArgEscape, etc.) until fixpoint, and can be done intraprocedurally per method with summary edges connecting at call sites, or fully interprocedurally by merging callee connection graphs into the caller (more precise but far more expensive, scaling with call-graph size and requiring either whole-program analysis or conservative assumptions at virtual/unresolved call sites).

**Stack allocation and scalar replacement of aggregates (SROA).** When escape analysis proves an allocation site's objects are NoEscape within a frame (never outlive the current method activation and aren't captured by closures/exceptions), the compiler can convert a heap allocation into a **stack allocation** (allocating inline in the stack frame rather than invoking the allocator/GC), or go further via **scalar replacement**: if, additionally, all accesses to the object's fields are statically resolvable (no escaping aliases, no reflection/unsafe access), the object's fields are replaced entirely by independent scalar SSA values/virtual registers, eliminating the allocation altogether. HotSpot C2 performs exactly this as part of its escape analysis pass (`EscapeAnalysis` + `MacroExpansion`/`PhaseMacroExpand` interplay), and Go's compiler performs analogous escape analysis to decide stack- vs heap-allocation of `make`/composite-literal results, directly reducing GC pressure by shrinking the set of objects the garbage collector must track.

**Elision of synchronization.** If escape analysis proves an object is thread-local (never reaches GlobalEscape, i.e., provably never observed by another thread), any `synchronized` block or monitor operation on that object is provably uncontended and can be elided entirely (lock elision), since no other thread can ever contend for that monitor. HotSpot C2 uses escape analysis results to drive this optimization, which is related to but distinct from **biased locking** (a runtime/JIT-cooperative optimistic locking scheme using a CAS-free fast path keyed on thread ownership bias, historically enabled by default but deprecated/removed in modern HotSpot [JDK 15+] partly because escape-analysis-based elision and other improvements reduced its benefit) — biased locking is a speculative runtime mechanism rather than a static proof, whereas EA-based lock elision is a sound static optimization when escape analysis's NoEscape/thread-local proof holds.

**Partial escape analysis with merge points (Graal).** Standard escape analysis is often all-or-nothing per allocation site: if any control-flow path lets the object escape, the whole object is heap-allocated on all paths. Graal's **partial escape analysis** (Stadler, Würthinger, Mössenböck) instead performs the analysis flow-sensitively through the control-flow graph, allowing an object to be treated as virtual (scalar-replaced, not materialized) along paths where it provably doesn't escape, and only **materializing** it (emitting the actual heap allocation and initialization) at the specific point where a path first causes it to escape — e.g., at a merge point where one incoming path keeps the object virtual and another requires it real, the object is materialized on the escaping branch and merged with the already-real object from other branches via a phi. This significantly increases applicability versus whole-method-conservative approaches, handling common patterns like objects allocated and usually consumed locally but occasionally stored into a field only under a rare branch.

**Interprocedural vs. intraprocedural precision limits.** Intraprocedural escape analysis (analyzing one method body at a time, treating calls to other methods conservatively, e.g., assuming any object passed to an unanalyzed callee becomes GlobalEscape) is cheap and composes well with JIT compilation units (HotSpot C2 analyzes within the current compilation's inlining tree, effectively getting interprocedural precision for inlined callees and falling back to conservative ArgEscape/GlobalEscape at call boundaries that aren't inlined). Fully interprocedural (whole-program) escape analysis gets better precision across non-inlined call boundaries but requires either a closed-world assumption (feasible in Go's static whole-program compilation model) or expensive call-graph summary computation/invalidation under dynamic dispatch and class loading (a major complication for Java JITs, which mitigate via speculative optimization backed by deoptimization if a previously-unseen subclass or reflective access violates the escape assumption). Precision is further limited by field sensitivity (tracking escape per-field vs. per-object — coarser field-insensitive analyses merge all fields' points-to information, increasing conservatism) and by aliasing (if two references may alias and one escapes, field/object-sensitive analyses must propagate escape state across all aliases, and imprecise alias analysis forces conservative GlobalEscape classification).
